full_judgment:
ARM Amirul Islam Chowdhury, J.: This Rule was issued calling upon the Deputy Commissioner, Moulvibazar and opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the Judgment and order dated 2.5.89 passed by the Sessions Judge, Moulvibazar in Miscellaneous Case No. III of 1989 should not be set aside and why the victim girl Sumati Begum (petitioner) should not be given in custody of her husband or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 One Rafique Ullah, maternal grandfather of victim girl Sumati Begum, lodged a First information Report with Maulvibazar Police Station on 3.4.1989 stating therein that few months ago accused Manik and others kidnapped his granddaughter Sumati Begum aged about 14/15 years from the house of Muslim, father of victim girl Sumati Begum in respect of which Muslim, father of victim girl Sumati Begum earlier lodged a First Information Report with Moulvibazar Police Station on 3.8.88 and the said police case was subsequently numbered as GR case No.86 of 1988 of the Court of Upazila Magistrate, Moulvibazar and after recovery of victim Girl Sumati Begum, she was given in Jimma to her maternal grandfather Rafiq Ullah. Thereafter on 17.3.89 when victim girl Sumati along with her maternal grandfather Rafiq Ullah was coming from the house of the mother of Sumati Begum on the way accused persons kidnapped victim girl Sumati Begum by force and accused persons confined her for immoral purpose. Subsequently the said PS case was numbered as GR case No. 32 of 1989. Thereafter on 11.8.89 victim girl Sumati Begum appeared before the Upazila Magistrate, Moulvibazar and prayed to allow her to go with her alleged husband Manik and to record her statement under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure but the Upazila Magistrate instead kept her in judicial custody and sent her to the local Jail. Thereafter Rafiqullah, the maternal grandfather of victim girl Sumati Begum filed an application before the Sessions Judge, Moulvibazar for giving victim girl Sumati Begum to his custody and the said application was registered as Misc. case No. 111 of 1989. Victim girl Sumati Begum also filed an application before the Sessions Judge Moulvibazar to allow her to go with her alleged husband Manik and the said application was registered as Misc. case No. 110 of 1989. The Sessions Judge Moulvibazar took up both the applications together for hearing but disposed of these by two separate judgments. The prayer of victim girl Sumati Begum to allow her to go to her alleged husband Manik was refused by the Sessions Judge. The Sessions Judge, however, on consideration of the materials before him by the impugned order gave victim girl Sumati Begum in the Jimma of her father Muslim. Being aggrieved by the impugned order dated 2.5.89 passed by the Sessions Judge, victim girl Sumati Begum moved this application under sections 439 and 491 of the Code of Criminal Procedure before this Court and obtained the present Rule. 

 4. The records of this case was called for and the same have been placed before us. Rafiquellah opposite party No. 1 (maternal grandfather of the victim girl) is contesting the Rule by filing a counter affidavit along with a certificate from the Head Master of the school where she was reading at the relevant time. School certificate shows that victim girl Sumati Begum was born on 5.6.75. So according to school certificate she would complete 16 years of her age on 4.6.91. According to the statement made by the father in the FIR dated 3.8.88 she was 14/15 years of age. Medical Board in its opinion dated 4.2.89 gave her age as 15/16 years. We are keeping the application dated 11.4.89 filed by the victim girl Sumati Begum before the Upazila Magistrate in GR case No. 86/88 stating her age as 20 years out of our consideration. On consideration of the materials placed before us there is no doubt that the victim girl Sumati Begum is over 16 years but has not completed 18th year of her age. 

 8. Mr. AKM Foiz, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner victim girl Sumati Begum referred to the cases reported in 15 DLR 148, 17 DLR 544, 35 DLR 315, 2 BCR 41, 1 BLD 469, 1990 BLD 85. In support of his contention that the victim girl on the basis of FIR dated 3.8.88 and the medical report dated 23.1.89 being above sixteen years of age be allowed to go wherever she desires. Mr. Nasiruddin Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party No. 1, maternal grandfather of the victim girl has relied on the decision reported in 10 BCR 44 and 42 DLR 79 in support of his contention that the victim girl being below 18 years of age is to be restored to her parent. 

 9. In the instant case there is no dispute that according to the FIR dated 3.8.88 and the medical report dated 23.l.89 the victim girl is over 16 years of age. The question before us is whether she (being not an accused in the case) he kept in judicial custody and be given to her parent or be set at her liberty. In the case of Sukhendra Chandra Das Vs. the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, reported in 42 DLR 79 a Division Bench comprising of Fazal Hossain Mohammad Habibur Rahman, and Mahmudul Amin Chowdhury JJ observed as follows: 

 "In the present case it has been stated above that prima facie at this state we take the view that she is a minor aged about 17 years born on 11.9.7l. This view will not prejudice the other party at the trial and the trial Court will be at liberty to determine the age on the basis of evidence. As the victim girl Ranjana Rani Das prima facie appears to be aged about 17 years born on 11.9.71 it is in the best interest of the victim girl that she remains in the custody of her father petitioner Sukhendra Chandra Das as the said father is the greatest well-wisher of the victim girl. She is at liberty to go wherever she likes when she attains the age of majority." 

 10. In the case of Krishna Pada Datta versus Ministry of Home Afairs reported in 10 BCR 1990 HCD 44 a Division Bench of this court comprising Fazle Hossain Mohammad Habibur Rahman and Habibul Islam Bhuiyan JJ (as he then was) observed as follows: 

 "We are in respectful agreement with the views expressed in Muthu Ibrahim's case ILR 37 Mad, 567 and in the case of Sukhendra Chandra Das, 42 DLR 79 that for the purpose of custody of the girl age of majority laid down in the Majority Act, 1875 read with Guardian and Wards Act, 1890 i.e. the age of 18 years is the determining factor to decide whether the girl is to be given to the custody of the guardian or that she is major. It is needless to state that reference to the age of sixteen in case of a female minor in section 361 of the Penal Code is only for the purpose of commission of the offence of kidnapping punishable under section like 363 of the Penal Code and not for the purpose of deciding whether the girl is sui juris." 

 12. In the case of Jahanara Begum @ Jotsna Rani Saha Vs. the State reported in 15 DLR 148 it was observed as under: 

 "In the present case, the father of the girl in the first information report stated the age of the girl to be 14 years and in a petition filed before the learned Magistrate for medical evidence of the girl stated her age to be 15 years on the 4th of December, 1961. The girl has stated that she is aged 18 years and this statement received support from the report of Civil Surgeon. It is true that the father challenged the finding of the Civil Surgeon and prayed for examination of the girl by the Medical Board. In view of the admission of the father himself, however, on the 4th of December, 1961, that her age was 15 years she must be more than 16 years now. In that view, we do not think it will be just to keep the girl in custody against her will particularly when she has not even been cited as a witness in the chargesheet," 

 13. In coming to the above conclusion Sattar J considered the case of Santipada Ganguli Vs. Sovarani Ganguli (Criminal Revisional case No. 360 of 1959 disposed on 25.6.59) wherein it was observed as under: 

 14. In the case of Amin Bux versus Meher Ali and ots. Wahiuddin Ahmed, J. on an application under section 491 CrPC filed by Amin Bux, the father of girl named MSL Sohini, who was found to be aged more than 14 years, allowed her to go wherever she liked. In the case of Muhammad Sharil, Vs. La! Muhammad and (5) Jamil Husain Rizvi. J., observed as under: 

 "In a case under section 363, PPC the police officer should apply for a warrant being issued by a Magistrate under section 100 CrPC and then produce the minor before the Magistrate for such orders as in the circumstances of the case, the Magistrate might deem proper. The abducted girl was no doubt a witness in the case but she cannot be detained against her will specially in the case of a legally wedded woman." 

 15. In the case of Kiran Bala Chowdhury versus the State reported in 17 DLR 544 a Division Bench comprising AS Chowdhury and Abdulla JJ observed as under: 

 16. In the case of Annada Mohan Banerjee Vs. State & others reported in 35 DLR 315 a Division Bench of this Court comprising Abdur Rahman Chowdhury and Md. Altaf Hossain 11 observed as under: 

 "It appears that she is above 16 years today. For the purpose of deciding question of petitioner's entitlement to the custody of the girl, the age which is relevant is the age on the date on which the question is decided. It has been held in the case of Jahanara Begum alias Jotsna Rani Shaha Vs. The State and another reported in 15 DLR 148 that "where a person is brought before the court is aged 16 years or over, the will of such person, when the question before the court is whether she or he should be detained or allowed to go from Court's custody, must be allowed to prevail. The position of such a person is, at the most that of a witness and therefore not being an accused she or he cannot be detained against her or his will". 

 "In this reported case, the father of the victim girl, who was alleged to be kidnapped stated her age to be 14 years in the FIR and 15 years in his petition filed before the Magistrate for medical examination of the girl. The Court found that she was on the admission of the father himself more than 16 years now, and held that it will not be just to keep the girl in custody against her will particularly when she has not even been cited as a witness. In Criminal Revision No. 522 of 1979 (Jesmin Sultana @ Manika Rani Vs. The State and another) decided by Division Bench of this Court (not yet reported) to which we ourselves were parties, it was held that as the girl was above 16 years of age as of today the Court did not see any reason to keep her in judicial custody against her will particularly when she was neither an accused nor has been cited as a witness in the FIR" 

 17. In the case of Sunil Kumar Chakraborty Vs. State and another reported in 2 BCR (1982) BCD page 41 (the judgment was delivered on 4th February, 1982) it was observed as under: 

 "The question before us is whether the girl is minor. It has been contended on behalf of the petitioner that in an application under section 439 CrPC this court should not determine the age of the girl and leave it to be determined at the trial on evidence to be led by the parties. In the instant case we do not like to determine the age of Kaberi Chakraborty, however, as she is not an accused in the case we feel that she should not be kept any more in judicial custody in jail. Her SSC certificate shows that she was born on 14.12.65. Whether the entry in the SSC certificate is correct or not could be decided only on evidence to be led by the parties at the trial. In the facts of the case we are inclined to release Kaberi Chakraborty on her own bond with two sureties. Accordingly we direct that Kaberi Chakraborty alias Tahmina Begum be released on her executing a bond with two sureties of Taka 5000.00 each to the satisfaction of the Deputy Commissioner, Dacca subject to the condition that she would be produced as and when required before the court concerned in connection with Ramna PS case No. 47 (12) 1981. 

 18. In the case of Pauma Begum Urmila Rani Vs. Gageswar Nath & the State reported in 9 BLD (1989) page 469 a Division Bench of this Court comprising of Md. Abdul Jalil and Qazi Shafiuddin JJ observed as follows: 

 "A Magistrate cannot detain a person unless her or she is as accused in a Criminal case but he has certain power under section 100 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Section 100 runs as follows: 

 If any Metropolitan Magistrate, Magistrate of the first class or sub-divisional Magistrate has reason to believe that any person is confirmed under such circumstances that the confinement amounts to an offence he may issue a search warrant and the person to whom such warrant is directed may search for the person confirmed; and such search be made in accordance therewith, and the person, if found, shall be immediately taken before a magistrate, who shall make such order as in circumstances of the case seems proper." 

 In the instant case the girl is shown to have been a victim of an offence of kidnapping or abduction under section 366 of the Penal Code. The word 'Kidnapping' has been defined in section 361 of the same Code which runs as follows: 

 In the case of Manindra Kumar Malakar Vs. Secretary Ministry of Home Affairs, & others reported in 10 131,1) 1990 page 85 a Division Bench comprising Latifur Rahman (as he then was) and Md. Mozammel Hoque JJ after consideration of several decisions observed as under: 

 "From the aforesaid decision it becomes clear that in a habeas corpus case like the present one their lordships were of the view that if the age of the victim girl is not found less than 16 years, then father guardian will not be entitled to claim her guardianship and the girl will be treated as major and she will be allowed to go anywhere she likes." 

 "100. If any Metropolitan Magistrate, Magistrate of the first class or Sub-divisional Magistrate has reason to believe that any person is confined under such circumstances that the confinement amounts to an offence, he may issue a search-warrant and the person to whom such warrant is directed may search for the person so confined; and such search shall be made in accordance therewith, and the person, if found, shall be immediately taken before a Magistrate, who shall make such order as in the circumstances of the case seems proper." 

 20. Decisions where it has been held that a female child who has completed 16 years of her age be not regarded as a minor and be allowed to go wherever she likes and could not be kept in custody relied mainly on section 552 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. We have considered the Children Act 1974 (hereinafter referred to as the Act), for the purpose of determining whether a female child above the age of 16 years could be given to the custody of her parent or any other person (unless she is an accused in a case). In this regard sections 2(f), 55, 56, 57, 58 and 61 of the Act are relevant (In the instant case victim girl Sumati Begum could at best be a witness in the case and not an accused). 

 (a) to be committed to a certified institute or an approved home until such child attains the age of eighteen years, or, in exceptional cases, for a shorter period, the reasons for such shorter period to be recorded in writing, or 

 22. Section 2(f) of the Act is of general application (both male and female). So are also sections 55, 56, 57, 58 and 61 of the Act. Section 552 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is applicable only in respect of a female child or woman) whereas the is applicable to both male and female child. The Act provides for the custody of a child against whom an offence has been committed or apprehended to be committed. Section 58 of the Act makes an elaborate procedure for the custody of victimised child. There is no difference under section 552 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, section 361 of the Penal Code and section 2(1) of the Act as to the age up to which a female child remains minor, under these provision of law a female child remains minor till she completes 16 years of age. The Penal Code does not provide for restoration of a minor to his or her guardian. Section 361 of the Penal Code merely provides as to when and how an offence of kidnapping punishable under section 363 is committed. Section 552 of the Code of Criminal Procedure provides for the restoration of a female child under the age of 16 years to her husband, parent, etc. Under section 552 of the Code of Criminal Procedure a female who has completed 16 years of her age must be allowed to go wherever she likes. Section 552 of the Code of Criminal Procedure does not provide for keeping a female child (woman) above 16 years of age in Custody. In other words a female child (woman) above 16 years of age cannot be kept or given in custody to any other person. Whereas the Act provides for an elaborate procedure for the custody of a minor child both male and female against whom an offence has been committed or apprehended to be committed even after he /she has completed 16 years of age. In other words child can be kept in custody for a certain time even after he/she has completed 16 years of age on consideration of sections 2(f), 55, 56, 57, 58 and 61 of the Act, We are of the opinion that if an offence is committed against a child before attaining 16 years of age, the court has the power to keep that child in custody till that child attains the age of 18 years, or till the proceeding in respect of the crime committed against the child is terminated in either conviction, discharge or acquittal. In the instant case an offence is alleged to have been committed against Sumati Begum while she was below 16 years of age. On the materials before us we are of the opinion that Sumati Begum is now above 16 years but below 18 years of age. It is submitted by Mr. Nasiruddin Chowdhury, that Muslim, father of Sumati in whose Jimma she was given by the Sessions Judge, Moulvibazar, is dead. In the circumstances we direct that victim girl Sumati Begum be given in the custody or Jimma of her mother on condition that her mother would produce her in the concerned court in connection with GR case No. 86 of 1988 and GR case No 32 of 1989 of the court of Upazila Magistrate, Moulvibazar as and when required to do so by the concerned courts.
